question: What is Netflix's theatrical window policy as of the 3Q26 call?
expected: Traditional 45-day window for a handful of films (e.g. Narnia), not all films as Sally Barton's note says.

result.answer:
As of the 3Q26 call, Netflix does not have a single standard theatrical window [1, 2, 3]. Sarandos said each film has its own "bespoke release pattern" and that Netflix is "a streaming first business" [1]. The windows he described vary by type of film: [1, 2, 3]
- Specialty releases: a 47-day platform theatrical window for La Bola Negra [2, 3]. Another specialty film, mosquito ball, gets a "bit shorter" window [2].
- IMAX release: for David Fincher's The Adventures of Cliff Booth, Netflix did a deal with IMAX for the biggest screens for a couple of weeks, 4 weeks before the Netflix release [2].
- Big family films: a 45-day window and a wide theatrical release for Greta Gerwig's Narnia: The Magician's Nephew and for Charlie versus the Chocolate Factory [2].

Sarandos summarized that the strategy now includes "a traditional 45-day window for a handful of films" [3]. Netflix also now reports box office grosses for its theatrical releases [3]. It expects about 30 theatrical releases this year, similar to last year [1].

Sally Barton's 3Q26 note is wrong on this point [1, 2, 3, 4]. It says Netflix is moving to "a standard 45-day theatrical window for all of its films" [4]. The transcript contradicts that [2, 3]. The 45-day window applies to a handful of films, and other releases have different windows [2, 3].

citations.passage: And yes, we're going to release about 30 films theatrically this year, pretty much what we did last year. And each 1 of these have their own kind of bespoke release pattern.
Now for those big family movies I talked about, we've already announced we have a 45-day window and a wide theatrical release for Greta Gerwig's new movie, Narnia, the Magician's Nephew.

It's involved to include a traditional 45-day window for a handful of films -- but the other 1 that's been important to folks is that we are also now reporting box office grosses for those releases when we do it.

question: What revenue growth did Netflix guide for 2027?
expected: No 2027 guidance given; deferred to the January (Q4) call, only 'strong revenue growth into 2027'.

result.answer:
Netflix did not give 2027 revenue growth guidance [1, 5]. On the 3Q26 call, CFO Spencer Neumann said it is "premature to issue full year 2027 guidance" and that Netflix would provide it on the Q4 call [1]. He also said 2027 guidance, including margin guidance, would come in January [2].

Management did give qualitative commentary [1, 3]. Netflix's "financial objectives are unchanged": it looks "to sustain double-digit revenue growth," expand margins and increase free cash flow [1]. Neumann also said Netflix expects "strong revenue growth into 2027" from three levers: member growth, pricing and ads [3].

For context, the only quantified guidance is for 2026: 13% to 14% top-line growth, roughly 12% FX neutral, as stated on the 2Q26 call [4]. The S&P table on the 3Q26 transcript lists "NA" under the guidance columns for FY2027 [5]. It gives a consensus revenue figure of about $56.9B [5].

The analyst notes agree [6]. Sally Barton's note says management deferred everything to January guidance [6].

citations.passage: So it's premature to issue full year 2027 guidance. We'll do that on our kind of next call on our Q4 call. But our financial objectives are unchanged. We look to sustain double-digit revenue growth.

We'll provide 2027 guidance in January, including that margin guidance, but there's no change to our philosophy of obviously, investing in our business to drive that growth in innovation and also steadily growing margin each year.
And we expect to deliver strong revenue growth into 2027 as well with those same three levers.

We expect to deliver another strong year with, as we saw -- as you see in the guide, 13% to 14% top line growth for the full year. That's roughly 12% FX neutral or about $6 billion of incremental revenue year-over-year.

question: What Azure growth did Microsoft guide to for FY27 Q2, and what did it say the guide depends on?
expected: 49-50% cc; depends on finding more efficiency gains beyond Q1's, plus token pricing / capacity uncertainty.

result.answer:
Microsoft guided FY27 Q2 (Oct–Dec 2026) Azure revenue growth to 49–50% in constant currency, per Amy Hood on the FY27 Q1 call. [1]

What the guide depends on (Hood):
- Efficiency gains: continued efficiency gains across the CPU and GPU fleet help offset some 3P GPU-as-a-service contracts that were delayed to H2. [1]
- More efficiency gains still to find: in Q&A she said Q1 efficiency gains continue into Q2, but "We need to find some more, which we're counting on" to reach the guide. [2]
- Supply timing: some supply Microsoft was counting on for Q2 moved out into H2. [2] She also said customer demand continues to exceed available supply. [1]
- Token pricing: she said there is "some unknown on some token pricing through the quarter." [2]
- Beyond Q2, year-over-year growth will keep reflecting the timing and scale of engineering efficiencies, new capacity adds, and a strong prior-year comparable. [1]

Analyst notes: Sally Barton's note gives the same 49–50% guide and the same dependencies, and calls the guide "less mechanical than usual" (her opinion). [3][4] Joe Smith's note also cites 49–50%. [5]

Errors in the notes (I checked only the figures that surfaced in my searches):

question: How did JPMorgan's full-year 2026 NII ex-Markets guidance change between the 1Q26 and 2Q26 calls, and why?
expected: ~$95B (held on 1Q) raised to ~$96.5B on 2Q, driven mainly by deposit balances rather than rates.

result.answer:
JPMorgan raised full-year 2026 NII ex-Markets guidance from about $95 billion (1Q26 call, where it was held unchanged) to about $96.5 billion (2Q26 call), a $1.5 billion increase [1][2][3].

Why, per Jeremy Barnum on the 2Q26 call:
- Deposit balances were the biggest single factor, across both Wholesale and Consumer [3]. He cited the overall quantum and a mix shift toward slightly higher-margin deposits [3].
- Rates were a little higher than when JPMorgan last guided, in both the short end and the back end [3]. He said JPMorgan's actual rate sensitivity is probably a bit more than the earnings-at-risk (EaR) figure suggests, because consumer betas outperformed the model, mostly at the front end [3].
- The new figure implies a higher exit run rate in the second half [3]. That assumes the yield curve follows current forwards and deposits and other drivers match current expectations [3].
- A small reclassification also played a part [4]. JPMorgan moved some equity allocation from Corporate to the CIB, so about $150 million of NII shifted out of NII ex-Markets into Markets NII [4].

Analyst notes:
- Joe Smith's notes agree with the transcript on both figures and on the deposit driver [5][6].
- Sally Barton's note also cites deposit balances as the main driver [7]. It states card NCO guidance rose to ~3.6%, but that is outside this question [7]. The transcript says the Card net charge-off rate was lowered to about 3.2%, so her figure is an error [8].

citations.passage: In terms of the full year 2026 outlook, we continue to expect NII ex. Markets to be about $95 billion.

In terms of the full year 2026 outlook, we now expect NII ex. Markets to be about $96.5 billion and total NII to be approximately $105.5 billion as a function of Markets NII increasing to about $9 billion.

Just mechanically in terms of the drivers of the upward revision, the biggest single factor is deposit balances, I would say, across both Wholesale and Consumer, both sort of the overall quantum of it, but also like mix shift inside of that in favor of slightly higher margin overall. And then, rates are like a little bit higher than when we previously guided both in the short-end and in the back-end.
And so, that NII is moving out of NII ex. into Markets NII.

result.answer:

question: Did JPMorgan raise its full-year 2026 expense guidance on the 1Q26 call?
expected: No - held at ~$105B (Joe Smith's note wrongly says raised to ~$107B). It was raised to ~$107.5B on the 2Q26 call.

result.answer:
No [1, 2, 3]. On the 1Q26 call JPMorgan kept its full-year 2026 adjusted expense outlook at about $105 billion [1]. CFO Jeremy Barnum said the outlook "continues to be about $105 billion" [1]. In Q&A he said the strong Markets and Banking performance might otherwise have led them to revise the guidance up [2]. He called the lack of a revision "a little early in the year" and said to "see how things play out in the next quarter or so" [2][3]. The increase came on the 2Q26 call, where the new adjusted expense outlook was about $107.5 billion [4]. That is up $2.5 billion from $105 billion [5].

Analyst note discrepancy: Joe Smith's 1Q26 note says management "raised the full-year adjusted expense guide to about $107B" on the 1Q26 call [6]. The transcript contradicts this, so the note is wrong [1, 2, 3]. The ~$107.5B figure came a quarter later [4]. Sally Barton's 1Q26 note correctly says the ~$105B guide was kept [7].

question: How fast is Netflix's advertising business growing in 2026?

result.answer:
Netflix's ads business is growing at over 80% in 2026, according to Gregory Peters on the 3Q26 call (Oct 2026) [1]. He said "We're still growing... our ads business over 80% this year." [1] The call gave no dollar ad revenue figure or quarterly ad growth rate.

Ads are growing but are behind plan [1]. Peters said Netflix set "big growth targets" for ads and is "currently a bit behind our aggressive target for the year." [1]

Ads are also one of three revenue levers (member growth, pricing, ads) that CFO Spencer Neumann said are all working [2]. He said they support "strong growth in 2026" and into 2027. [2] Full-year 2026 total revenue growth is guided to 13–14%, about 12% FX-neutral. [3]
